corrections.source_says: Set to yes for the randomized AI-configuration comparisons. Study 3 analyzed 769 writers who experienced Prompting, Reranking, and No Intervention in randomized order, and independent readers scored the originality of their paragraphs. This satisfies all three codebook criteria. The observational classification remains appropriate specifically for pooled AI-versus-earlier-unaided contrasts; it does not exclude the randomized comparisons among AI configurations.

The funnels distinguish non-completion from subsequent list-wise deletion, but do not specify individual writer dropout reasons. For Study 4, 804 readers completed and 802 remained after deletion; for Study 5, 8,010 completed and 7,996 remained. The reader deletions are attributed to incomplete data due to technical errors.

These are ratings, consistent with unit=rating, and must not replace the writer counts. Study 1's preferred subset contains 7,590 paragraphs; the retained distinct-writer counts for the preferred subsets are not supplied in these analyses.

corrections.source_says: The form omits rated paragraph clarity, informativeness, and relevance, which are output-quality outcomes under the codebook's usefulness construct. Add these outcomes for both Studies 1 and 3. Study 1 preferred-subset AMEs are clarity 8.978 (95% CI [8.669, 9.287]), informativeness 22.744 ([22.341, 23.146]), and relevance 8.307 ([8.035, 8.579]). Study 3 reports the corresponding outcomes for each mitigation configuration relative to human-written paragraphs in Tables S256, S257, and S259. These are human ratings on 0?100 scales.
corrections.quote: It elevated perceived writing quality, with paragraphs judged as clearer (+9.0), more informative (+22.7), and more relevant (+8.3).

corrections.source_says: Fill the required diversity methods: distributional spread of reader ratings across human-written versus AI-written paragraphs, using SD for 0?100 attributes and base-2 Shannon entropy for categorical attributes; differences are model minus writer. Uncertainty comes from a nonparametric bootstrap with 1,000 resamples and Bonferroni correction across 29 attributes. No embedding model is used. The described method does not state the bootstrap resampling unit, so that detail remains unknown; do not infer writer-level clustering. This analysis was not preregistered.
corrections.quote: We assess statistical significance using a nonparametric bootstrap procedure with n=1,000 resamples, applying Bonferroni correction across all 29 rating attributes.

confirmed: Source identification is correct: the local PDF is arXiv:2604.22503v2, dated 29 Jun 2026, with 20 pages (main PDF p. 1 and PDF page count). I read the complete local markdown, including references, and checked the numerical claims against PDF text/tables. The separate SI fetched in memory from the form's pinned repository URL is dated June 25, 2026 and has 192 pages (SI p. 1 and PDF page count).

Studies 1 and 3 contain randomized AI-configuration assignments to writers, supporting online_rct and has_randomized_people_study=true. Study 3 explicitly randomizes condition order and obtains originality ratings on participants' edited writing (main pp. 12?14, ??4.4, 4.6, 4.10; SI pp. 7?8, ?1.3; p. 32, ?2.7).

The pooled AI-versus-unaided contrasts have a fixed unaided-then-AI sequence, correctly described as observational context in the form's reason. All unaided paragraphs precede AI engagement (SI pp. 15?17, ?2.3; pp. 28?31, ??2.5?2.6).

Writer counts at first treatment assignment and after exclusions match: Study 1, 1,532 and 1,501; Study 2, 681 and 669; Study 3, 809 and 769. These count people, and no writing study has fewer than 50 analyzed writers (SI pp. 9?11, Tables S14, S16, S17).

Study 1 input-condition counts match: stance-based 1,501, bullets-based 1,501, rewrite 740, improve 761. Each writer encounters each of the three input formats once, so the paragraph-variant observations correspond to writers assigned that variant; these are overlapping within-person arms (SI p. 7, ?1.3; p. 44, Table S21).

Study 2 analyzed disclaimer-arm counts of 160, 154, and 185 are printed in the main PDF p. 13, ?4.9. The no-disclaimer count of 510 in SI p. 7, Table S11 counts writer?proposition observations, so leaving its unprinted people count null follows the no-inference rule. Study 2 did not collect third-party ratings of its paragraphs (main p. 12, ?4.6; SI p. 29, ?2.5).
All 769 analyzed Study 3 writers experienced No Intervention, Prompting, and Reranking; they are not separate groups of 769 people (main p. 13, ?4.10; SI p. 8, ?1.3 and Table S12).

All numbers in S1-O1.reported match Table S41: AME 12.467, 95% CI [12.102, 12.831]; OR 1.708, 95% CI [1.682, 1.735]; z=67.265; p printed as 0. These are preferred-subset rating-level beta-regression results with reader random intercepts (SI p. 69, Table S41; p. 62, ?5.6).

All numbers in S1-O2.reported match: 22 of 29 attributes have lower dispersion at p<.001 after Bonferroni correction (main p. 4, ?2.2). For writer confidence, Table S183 prints writer SD 24.05, model SD 20.48, difference ?3.57, 95% CI [?3.81, ?3.31], ratio 0.852, and ***. This measures rating dispersion rather than semantic similarity of ideas (SI p. 120, ?5.9 and Table S183).

All numbers in S3-O1.reported match Table S258: Reranking AME 12.716, 95% CI [11.661, 13.770]; No Intervention AME 13.380, 95% CI [12.352, 14.409]. Each is relative to human-written paragraphs; that table does not print a direct Reranking-minus-No-Intervention estimate or interval (SI p. 151, ?8.4; p. 155, Table S258).

The one-line finding accurately reproduces the originality estimate and homogenization summary, including the fixed-order qualification (main p. 4, ?2.2; SI p. 69, Table S41). AMEs are points on the original rating scale, not standardized creativity effects (main p. 13, ?4.7; SI pp. 24 and 32, rating scales).

Studies 4 and 5 analyzed 802 and 7,996 readers and randomized exposure to existing paragraphs, without assigning writing assistance to those readers; other is appropriate for this creativity screening (SI p. 8, ?1.3; p. 12, Tables S19?S20; pp. 178 and 184, ??9.2 and 10.2).

The three writer samples total 2,939 distinct writers. Reader samples overlap across Studies 1 and 3: 1,469 readers took part in both; this does not imply writer overlap (main p. 11, ?4.1; SI p. 4, ?1.2).
This is a primary empirical paper with five studies, not a synthesis; the blank synthesis defaults are appropriate (main p. 11, ?4 Methods).
summary: Study 3 randomized AI configurations for 769 writers and scored paragraph originality, so the paper qualifies for the randomized-people pipeline. The reported estimates and participant counts match the PDFs, but core eligibility and several omitted study, outcome, and methods fields require correction.
